utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Our first witness for this week is Major Darko Gelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major Gelic, we have provided the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him give his full name and details in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your name is Darko Gelic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am Darko Gelic. I was born 23rd September 1965 in Zenica. I'm married and have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Major, you have prepared an outline of the testimony that you propose to give today, and I believe that you have signed that outline on the 29th of April of this year. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, unless I'm told otherwise, if I may, just for the purpose of expediency, I propose to lead Major Gelic through most of this, which should be relatively uncontroversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No doubt you'll know what the controversial areas are. Certainly the background can be led briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, and I would appreciate if the Prosecution would indicate for me which paragraphs they do not want me to lead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, is it the case that you did your national military service in the Yugoslav People's Army in 1983; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And following your completion of your national service requirements, you left the JNA and went to school for several years?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I understand that you were a member of the Territorial Defence in Zenica before the establishment of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you are one of the Bosnian Croats in Zenica who left the Territorial Defence to join the HVO once it was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just tell the Court approximately how many of the former Bosnian Croat members of the Territorial Defence actually left that organisation to join the HVO once it was established in the spring of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, in the TO units at that time there were not many Croats. But out of the number that were there, about 90 per cent of Croats, to my recollection, left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, Major Gelic, I believe that you were a company commander in the TO in the village of Broda, just outside of Zenica. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the outskirts of the city of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And could you tell the Court what you did after you joined the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: After I stopped working at the Territorial Defence, when we established ourselves as the HVO, I was first commander of the reconnaissance company. And then in June 1992, before the Jure Francetic Brigade was established, I was appointed chief of the intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And when exactly did you join the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I joined the HVO in early April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And after the formation of the Jure Francetic Brigade, what were your functions within that brigade, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Throughout my tour with the brigade, I was at first the commander of the reconnaissance company and then the chief of the intelligence service. And once the brigade was fully established in December 1992, I was again reappointed chief of the intelligence service for the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. We'll get into this in a little bit more detail later in your testimony, Major, but is it right that the Bosnian Croats and the HVO were attacked by Muslim armed forces in the city of Zenica on the 17th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I think it's a fact that the two Zenica brigades, the two Zenica-based HVO brigades, were defeated after just a few days of fighting, and you were subsequently forced to flee southwards to the town of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just give the Court a thumbnail sketch, sir, of what you did for the HVO once you arrived in Vitez in, I guess it was, late April, early May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after I arrived in Vitez, I became an advisor for the intelligence service in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. I stayed in that post for about 45 days, and then I was appointed a liaison officer with UNPROFOR and other international organisations, including the ECMM, UNHCR, International Red Cross, and other organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that you served in that position from June of 1993 until January the 18th of the following year, 1994.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And what did you do after January the 18th of 1994, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: After 18 January 1994, I was appointed chief of the intelligence department of the 3rd Guards Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in that position, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In this post, I stayed until 1998, when I was appointed a deputy commander of the 3rd Guards Brigade for the civil/military affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe that you currently serve in the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, holding the rank of Major.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, as I said, I am assistant commander for civil and military affairs for the 3rd Guards Brigade, and I hold the rank of Major in the army of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Major. Turning to paragraph 10 of the summary that you signed, I'd just like to ask a few questions about the initial organisation of the HVO in Zenica. Could you just give the Court a brief description of the circumstances under which the HVO was formed in Zenica and the background behind the decision of the Bosnian Croats, who were formerly members of the TO, to leave that organisation and join the HVO, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, after the outbreak of the civil war in our country, that is, in March and April 1992, after the general chaos broke out, I took part in the negotiations between the TO, and the discussions were about the armaments for the Bosnian Croats that served in the TO. And I was also part of the negotiation team to form a joint command of the armed forces. The purpose of the negotiations was to form a joint command of the armed forces, but this was not going as we had thought that it would. We could not achieve the results which we wanted and what the other groups in Bosnia wanted to get, weapons to organise units so that we could fight for the liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In most of these negotiation sessions, Mr. Jasmin Saric was a representative of the TO and later the commander of the town of Zenica, and based on all the statements which he made at the time during those negotiations, it was clear that we were not getting what we wanted. We never received any weapons. And the argument that the Muslim side offered was that the Croats could not get any weapons. And then in Broda, which is one of the communities on the edge of Zenica, the Croats there held a meeting where we wanted to define things and figure out what to do. And the conclusion was that we had to give up the idea of joining the Territorial Defence and that we had to establish ourself as a Croat force in order to be able to defend our own people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Saric take the position that Bosnian Croats would not be permitted the distribution of any of the arms located in the former JNA barracks in the city of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, in essence, he publicly never stated that, but from the context in which we were discussing things, this was not the conclusion which only I reached; everybody reached that conclusion, that the Muslim side did not want to give any weapons to the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 11 of the summary, and just a few questions in connection with the military organisation of the HVO. What kind of organisational structure did the HVO have in the earliest days of its organisation, in April, May, June, and July of 1992, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The organisation of the Croatian Defence Council at first was very poor. The Croatian Defence Council was not really organised, so that there were a lot of problems and it couldn't function properly. Obviously, after July 1992 the organisational structure of the HVO armed forces became much clearer because it was much more firmly established, and the chain of command which was then established was much clearer and you could say that the chain of command at that time was actually functional.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In 1992, sir, who was the commander-in-chief in the HVO general staff in the Mostar area?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In 1992 the commander of the HVO in Mostar was Brigadier Milivoj Petkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And who was the military commander in the Central Bosnia region, as far as you can recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The commander at the time was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And it's correct, is it not, that the military organisation that was imposed by the general staff was for so-called operative zones to be performed in particular areas where the HVO had armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, starting in July, approximately, of 1992, the HVO was restructured and persons to order the brigades were established with their commands and staffs of these commands, down to the lowest level of command. So all these people were appointed to these positions down this chain. I can mention some examples, like Busovaca, Zenica, Travnik, where these brigades, by such orders, were established. They were replenished inasmuch as it was possible, but all the command staff was appointed at that time by orders from the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Staying at the operative zone level for just a second, Major, in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone you've identified the commander as Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, at least from July of 1992 onwards. I take it he reported directly to his commanding officer, Brigadier Petkovic at the HVO general staff headquarters.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then you've talked about the establishment of brigades. Is it correct that these brigades were generally municipality-based and that they drew their soldiers from the municipalities in which they were based?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Of course, as I previously stated, all the brigades which were established were established on the territorial principle, where each unit was established in the municipality where it was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the brigade commanders, of course, reported in turn to their commanding officer, the commander of the operative zone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And so in Zenica, for example, I think it's correct to say that Commander Zivko Totic was the commander of the HVO forces in that city, and he reported directly in the chain of command to his commanding officer, Colonel Blaskic, commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And once the brigades were established, sir, is it correct that they had their own chain of command and that the positions within those brigades were generally filled?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, can you tell us whether, to your knowledge, Mr. Dario Kordic ever occupied any position within the military chain of command, either in the HVO or within the Busovaca Brigade, the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You actually yourself assumed a position within the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone when you became a liaison officer, liaising with UNPROFOR, the ECMM, and the UNHCR and other international organisations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you ever, throughout your time in the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, see Mr. Kordic perform any military function?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning Your Honours to paragraph 13 of the summary, could you just give us, sir, your testimony regarding the relative armed strengths of the Muslim and Croat armed formations in the city of Zenica, where you were initially located before mid-April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's not much point in the witness simply reading out the answers that are in paragraph 13 unless he can give some foundation for his knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just give us a short answer on that, please. What do you know about it, and tell us how you know about it too.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, regarding the HVO weaponry in Zenica, it was not only inferior in comparison to that of the ABiH, but we were very poorly armed in comparison with the Muslim side. This knowledge is my personal knowledge, because I worked on arming the Croatian people in the Zenica area. There's another question, how much I succeeded in this, in arming Croats, but the percentage of weapons of Croats in the HVO units in Zenica area was about 30 per cent level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Approximately how many semi-automatic and automatic rifles were available to your armed formations, the HVO armed formations in the city of Zenica throughout the time that you were there, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In total, the Zenica HVO at that time had about 300 pieces of weapons, that is, between the automatic and semi-automatic rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did the ABiH have control over former military facilities run by the JNA in that city, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court approximately how many rifles were stored in the military barracks and facilities that were formally run by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: After the liberation of the Zenica barracks from the former JNA during that liberation, and both Croats and Muslims participated in this, we took about 10.000 automatic and semi-automatic rifles, a number of anti-aircraft guns, a number -- I believe about 17 tanks. Most of them were T-55 model. But all of these weapons in that barracks went to the Muslim side. Perhaps a small part, and I say a very small part, may have gone to Croats. But I'm talking about stuff that was in the barracks. After the fall of the barracks, it was taken to the steel works in Zenica, where it was kept, and later on it was distributed to the TO units and the ABiH units, while the Croat side, that is, the HVO, never received any part of that, of this package, if I can call it so, that was in that barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You made some reference to tanks that were formerly controlled by the JNA forces and taken over by the ABiH. What happened to those tanks, as best you can recall, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Those tanks -- that is, a number of those tanks were not in working order. They tried to fix them, but a small number were deployed. I think one or two were in the Usora area and one or two were deployed in the Visoko area in order to help them in defence of those areas. But the rest of them remained in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to the subject of persecution, sir -- paragraph 14 of the outline, for the Court's information -- the contention is made in this case that the Bosnian Croats and, specifically, the Bosnian Croat political leadership, advocated and enforced a policy of persecution and harassment of Muslim civilians by the HVO in the municipality of Zenica and also in the municipalities that made up the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Were you ever aware of such a policy, sir? Did you ever hear of anything like that? Could you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, to me it sounds absurd. Never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, don't comment. If you will keep your answers to the facts, Mr. Gelic.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we never were issued such an order, nor did we ever have such a policy in place, to persecute Muslims in that area. In fact, Croats in that region were subject to this, and I can only say that this was a policy that was conducted against the Croats by Muslims. But I am not aware of any official or unofficial order or any other form of document. I have never heard of any such direction to persecute Muslims and drive them out of the region of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, is the allegation that there was a policy of persecution or that there was, in fact, persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think the allegation in paragraph 36 of the amended indictment, Your Honour, is that there was a policy of persecution and that there was persecution in fact. Both things are alleged. I was just dealing with the policy issue with Major Gelic, and with the Court's permission, I'll just address the persecution-in-fact allegations in the municipality of Zenica right now. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You had your microphone on, Your Honour. I thought you were going to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major Gelic, as a matter of fact, is it the case that Bosnian Muslims outnumbered Bosnian Croats in the municipality of Zenica in 1993, anyway, approximately six to one?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the ratio was perhaps a little lower, three to one or four to one. But when the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina, after the Muslims were expelled from the areas where they had lived, that is, where the Serbs expelled them, then there was a large inflow of refugees in the town of Zenica, so that that figure -- that is, that ratio of three to one or four to one rose to six to one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you heard the Judge's question regarding whether, in fact, Bosnian Croats persecuted Bosnian Muslims in the municipality of Zenica and throughout the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Could you give us, sir, your experience in that regard? Did Croats persecute Muslims or was it the other way around?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As far as my experience goes, Your Honours, it was quite the other way around. I remember the first expelled Croat from that area under -- if I may call it that, controlled by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croat Defence Council, because we were still together at the time, and that was May, maybe June -- no, May, the first Croat was expelled then from the area of Nemila or, rather, Bistricak. I believe his last name was Kovacevic. He and his family were expelled from the area, even though there was no conflicts at all between the Muslims and the Croats. I was then ordered by my commander, Mr. Zivko Totic, to go to the area and investigate the matters and what could have been the immediate cause for expelling this Croat family from there. I went there. I could not gain access to that particular locality for the simple reason that a military camp had been set up there and in it were quartered, from what I could see, foreign citizens who had come to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is, the Mujahedin. They were quartered in that area, and they would not allow anyone to get there. Why were they expelled from the area? I think that that family was simply in the way. It was the only Croat family there, and it was in the way. They thought that it might obstruct their training or whatever they wanted to do or, rather, to expel all the Croats from the territory of Zenica at a later stage. So that is the beginning of 1992, that is, May or, rather, late of May, and that was the Croats were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just a couple of formal questions in this connection, sir. Did you ever receive any orders from your military commander, Commander Totic, or from anybody else in the military chain of command to harass or persecute anyone?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. I've already said so when His Honour corrected me. There were no orders, official or off-the-record, or any act, any document, that might bear on such a matter. There was absolutely no order to engage in the persecution or expulsion of Muslims or Serbs, for that matter, from the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's depart from formal orders for just a minute. Did you ever hear anybody, either politician or soldier, advocate the commission of acts of violence, or harassment, or persecution against any non-Croat ethnic group throughout the time that you were in the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As I have already said, there was nothing. Not an official nor an unofficial example existed, persecution of Muslims, or Serbs, let alone Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. Sayers. I should like to ask the witness about what he understands, what he means. How does he define "persecution" that he speaks about?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, how would I define -- what do I mean by "persecution" when I say that? It is when you expel somebody, when you evict somebody from his home, when you force him to leave the place where he's lived. That is what "persecution" means to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. So according to you, nobody was forced to leave their place where they had lived, according to you; there was no document, there was no act to that effect, to force anybody to leave?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You mean the Croat Defence Council, do you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because that was the question which Mr. Sayers was asking you.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, quite so. As I already said, there was neither an official nor an unofficial document which would be regulating that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the question that you were asked was beyond documents, whether in fact you could see anything of that nature which one could call persecution. I'm not talking about documents. Apart from the documents but, in point of fact, on the ground, in reality.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe I am repeating it for the second time. There was neither an official or unofficial policy in the military structure. That is, in the military structure, there was neither an official or unofficial policy to evict people from their houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me tackle this another way, Major Gelic, and maybe this will address the questions the Court has been asking you. Did you ever hear any advocacy by any soldier or politician about giving Muslims generally a hard time, harassing them, for example, during their daily lives, blowing up their businesses, things of that variety? Have you ever heard of anything like that being recommended, or advocated, or urged by any soldier or politician?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You give one example, Major, in your outline of Bosnian Croats being given a pretty hard time by Muslim police in Zenica in May of 1992. Rather than me putting words in your mouth, could you just tell the Court, in your own words, what happened in May of 1992, insofar as you can remember?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, to begin with, the Croats who were there in Zenica were truly exposed to harassment, to intimidation, and all sorts of other things by Muslims in Zenica. In May, for example -- and I will quote that example -- in May 1992 the Muslim police tried to orchestrate the roundup of their criminals, because in their units there were many such men. So they organised a kind of arrest of those criminals. But that happened -- of course, the commander of the then municipal headquarters of the HVO in Zenica, what was the reason for that arrest, I really would not know. I think it was all a frame-up, it was all orchestrated, it was all thought up in order to provoke an armed incident between Muslim and Croat forces in that area through that operation of catching the criminals, as they called it. But owing to the presence of the Croats, the incident did not break out at that particular moment. However, a lesson could be drawn from that, and that meant that we, the Croats in Zenica, were no longer welcome in that town and there was no room for us in the town anymore, even though it was our town just as much as it was theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I believe there was an incident involving your wife, who was pregnant at the time in May of 1992. Could you tell the Court, in your own words, what happened to her, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, Your Honours, to begin with, it is really not agreeable to remember those things, but that was the truth at the time. We were trying to, as much as possible, fight against the Serb forces while there was still time for that, and when the Serb or, rather, the air force, the air force of the former Yugoslav People's Army or the Bosnian Serbs, whoever it belonged to at the time, when they shelled more or less at specific intervals, that is, there would be a day or two without such shelling in Zenica but there would be somewhere else, and during one of those shelling spells, when the target of the Serb planes was the steel works in Zenica, so the alarm was sounded. People had to withdraw to shelters. My wife was pregnant. My wife was expecting at the time. She was five months' pregnant. And Muslim military police stopped her somewhere on the fourth floor of the building where we used to live, made her go back to the flat in which we lived to allegedly search that flat, because somebody, according to them, was in that flat, that is, a Serb sniper or something like that. However, they knew very well whose apartment that was, and when they entered the flat, they once again drove my wife out of the flat because they did, in the flat, what they wanted to, and the shelling went on all that time. I lived in the immediate vicinity of the building which is near the Zenica steel works. The detonations were really on a large scale. And to do such a thing towards an expecting woman, my wife, it was beyond comprehension. Under those conditions -- so this is just one of such instances. Another such example or, rather, what happened to me, I told about that to my commander, Zivko Totic, hoping that he would undertake some steps with the Muslim side. And I think he turned it into a public issue, who is expelling whom from what areas, because it was quite -- what was happening in Zenica was quite conspicuous in that part. And when it happened to my wife, it didn't happen only to my wife, to my wife alone, it happened to all the Croats who lived in that building. My commander, as I've said, turned it into a public issue, informed the media which were within the Croat Defence Council, and I believe that -- what I have told you right now, I believe that Mr. Dario Kordic also raised it at a press conference when again journalists asked him about what was happening to Croats and with Croats in Zenica; not only Zenica, that is, but also in other parts of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just turning back to the incident where your wife was evicted, what happened to the personal possessions that you and your wife had in the apartment from which she was evicted, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, all our belongings, all the personal affairs were looted, not only mine, but everything that belonged to Croats in that building. The Muslim side simply availed itself of the shelling by the Serb troops and they simply availed themselves of the opportunity and simply plundered everything they could find in our flats. Naturally, they couldn't take furniture or things like that. They took personal belongings or whatever they happened to like.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just move on, Major, to the next subject, which is Mr. Kordic, who's one of the defendants in this case. I think you've already stated that he did not have the authority to give military orders, in your view. But let me just ask you this: Throughout your involvement in the armed forces of the HVO, did you ever see Mr. Kordic or hear of him actually giving any military orders, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kordic's function, sir? What was his position, as far as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, I think it was a political position. He was part of the political structure and that was the kind of duties that he discharged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You realised that he was one of the vice-presidents of the presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, is that right, or didn't you know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, the political offices, I wasn't particularly familiar with that, was he the president or vice-president. I don't really know what kind of offices they had in the HDZ organisation. I was not familiar with that, because I was a military man, and to begin with, I was not even allowed to engage in politics. And secondly, I was never all that interested in politics to try to learn about such things: who held what office and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me move on fairly quickly through this, in light of that testimony. Mr. Kordic was, I believe, sometimes called a colonel in the press. What was your understanding of his function as a colonel and the nature of his duties in that position, if any?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, I think it was a kind of an honorary rank conferred upon him. As far as I remember, there were some negotiations between Muslim Serbs and Croats in Sarajevo. Now, what the negotiations were about, I don't know, but I think that was the reason why he had to be accorded a military rank, so that he could parry properly other parties to these negotiations so that he could act as a counterpart, and I believe that was part of it. But I think that that was merely an honorary title.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the mixed military Working Group negotiations that occurred or were held in Sarajevo airport under the auspices of UNPROFOR at the end of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Now, what was it called, I don't really know whether it was mixed or what. I don't know. But that was a group which operated under the auspices of UNPROFOR. It was in 1992, I believe. There were those negotiations conducted at the Sarajevo airport, or at least that's what I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, were you ever asked by members of the International Community about the military chain of command within the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Why, yes. I don't know what period of time you mean. Do you mean 1992 or 1993? Because in 1993 I had very many contacts with the International Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just turn you to 1992. Do you recall a discussion that you had with two Spanish representatives of the International Community who visited Central Bosnia and asked you questions about the military chain of command and the political hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were Spanish representatives who came there for different matters, including intelligence reasons. And they wanted to talk to me and a commander in the HVO, and they also talked to the Muslim side. But when they came to see me, they asked me to first explain to them the command, the chain of command in our army. And since my superiors had advised me to receive those people, I explained to them the chain of command and structure of the Croat Defence Council, or rather I used my brigade as the example and the immediate superior of our brigade, or rather the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, which was Colonel Tihomir Blaskic. And after such discussion, I told them about the chain of command and the matter of functioning of the Croat Defence Council. But they also wanted to discuss some political matters, and they asked to see somebody who would be at the top of the policy pursued in Central Bosnia, that is, to have a discussion. And I consulted my commander, Zivko Totic, and I was then asked to take them first to the HDZ in Zenica to see Mr. Sarkic. But they were not really willing to discuss it at a local level, that is, with Mr. Sarkic. They asked for a higher level. And then I tried to arrange a meeting for them with Mr. Dario Kordic, and I believe they had half an hour, perhaps an hour with him. I waited for them while they were with him, and after that we went back to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic have any military authority over any units of the military police or any special purpose units in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, as far as you knew, at any time during your service in the HVO, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever see Mr. Kordic give orders to Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that Mr. Kordic had ever tried to give orders to Mr. Blaskic or influence his military decisions in any way, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In connection with Mr. Kordic's public activities, is it correct that he did give speeches to soldiers, trying to raise their morale and encourage recruitment efforts so that soldiers would enlist in the HVO and go to fight on the front lines at Jajce against the BSA?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We could not hear the beginning of the answer.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Not against the Bosnian Muslims

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- the question, and for that I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you just give us an assessment, as far as you saw it, Major Gelic, of the level of Mr. Kordic's influence, if any, in the city of Zenica, or the municipality of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, insofar as Mr. Kordic is concerned, and his influence, political influence in the town of Zenica, I believe it was considerable. And from the moral point of view, yes, he could affect, he could influence Croats who lived in Zenica. Moral, I say, because that was the only way that Zenica Croats could help. What influence he had with other people, I know he enjoyed the trust of many people as a politician, and thanks to the manner in which he spoke at the time, and I can say only the best about Mr. Dario Kordic while I still lived in Zenica. And when I was expelled from it, when I had to leave it and came to Vitez, I continued to have a very high opinion of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But as a practical matter, did he actually have any power to influence the plight of Bosnian Croats in the municipality of Zenica, one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. As I have said, yes, he could offer moral support, but nothing else. He could not do it in any other way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one final question along these lines. Did Mr. Kordic have any power to remove Colonel Blaskic from his position of command in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who had the power to remove Operative Zone commanders from their commands, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but it could not be Mr. Kordic. It had to be somebody who made part of the military chain of command. In 1992, for instance, it was Mr. Milivoj Petkovic, so he could replace a commander of the Operative Zone. After that, Mr. Praljak, then Mr. Roso. That is, all those commanders of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council could replace the commanding officers, but nobody else could do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see if we can move a little bit more quickly, Major. Were you aware that there was a brief outbreak of fighting in the Novi Travnik area in June of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'm looking at paragraph 22 of the outline now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of that conflict, and according to my knowledge at that time, I worked for the intelligence services in the Jure Francetic Brigade, so we had the intelligence information traffic. It was very limited in scope. It lasted one day. And this took place in June of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You just said, Major, that you believed that you worked for the intelligence service of the Jure Francetic Brigade, but this was June of 1992. Are you sure that the Jure Francetic Brigade existed at that time, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: At that time the Jure Francetic Brigade did not exist at the time, but there was an HVO headquarters in Zenica. This was in 1992. We were working on the organisation, which is why I brought up the name of Jure Francetic Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, turning, or going forward in time just a few months, to October of 1992, the Court has already heard about an armed roadblock that was erected by the ABiH at Ahmici on October 18th, 1992. And in that roadblock a troop convoy containing volunteers from Kresevo, Kiseljak, Busovaca, and elsewhere was stopped. Where was that troop convoy heading, Major Gelic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, at the time there was heavy fighting in the territory of Jajce municipality and all the volunteers from Central Bosnia, which includes Zenica, Kresevo, Fojnica, Vares, Kakanj, Vitez, Novi Travnik, Travnik, all these municipalities that were there, which were part of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, volunteers went to fight the Bosnian Serbs. In that same period, the situation in Jajce was very difficult. I can tell you this because I was there on three times. In fact, on the third time I was supposed to go there in order to help the Croats who were fighting for bare survival in that territory. But in October 1992 we were unable to pass through this area to go to Jajce, because at Ahmici a checkpoint had been set up by the Bosnian Muslims. And in my view, they staged this conflict in Novi Travnik in order to block our units from going to Jajce. And the excuse was that we were going to reinforce our forces in Novi Travnik, which was not true. In fact, my unit, which was sent from Zenica to Novi Travnik, went back to Zenica, and then they tried again to go via Travnik and on to Zenica, but we were not able to do so, because even there they tried to block us. That was at Lokvine. We couldn't pass through to go to Jajce. And so the result of that was -- is known to everyone. Jajce fell to the Bosnian Serbs, and the Croats who lived in that region were driven out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it true that about the same time the armed forces of the ABiH seized control of the Bratstvo arms factory in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And following that, Major, did the HVO ever manage at any time during the ensuing one and a half years of war to re-establish control of the Bratstvo factory at all?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. It never managed to reassert its control, and in fact I can add that the Bosnian Muslims took over all key armament factories. Konjica, Zenica, Tuzla, and Bratstvo is included, then Bugojno. The only thing that they were missing was Vitezit. And their objective -- and this is what I referred to when I talked about October 1992 and the tragedy at Jajce -- was to gain control over these military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mentioned the fact that the ABiH controlled other military facilities, and you specifically mentioned Konjic and Bugojno, I believe. Is it a fact that the Konjic arms factory manufactured bullets for small arms?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only the Konjic factory. There were also resources in Zenica, where small arms ammunition was also manufactured. And I note that there was also one in Babine, near Crkvica. They also produced shells, that is, parts of explosive devices. But in the steel works at Zenica, there was -- a lot of production facilities could be easily converted for military use.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And the factory in Zenica, I believe, was called -- forgive my appalling pronunciation -- Zeljezara; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Zeljezara, or steel works.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that was controlled by the ABiH forces in Zenica throughout the war, I take it, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've also mentioned the arms manufacturing facility in Bugojno. Is it correct that that facility manufactured detonators for artillery projectiles, fuses?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: According to my knowledge, yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Bratstvo arms factory, just to complete this line of questions, I believe manufactured the projectiles themselves for heavy artillery and heavy artillery pieces as well?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, speaking as a soldier, Major Gelic, could you give your views on the appropriateness or lack of appropriateness of the selection of Ahmici as the point where the armed roadblock was erected in October of 1992 by the ABiH, by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: From the military standpoint, the location where the roadblock was erected, that is, at the cemetery in Ahmici, was a very good position to -- because it cut off the Busovaca and Vitez municipality. It is a choke point, and with a very small force you could stop a much larger force, regardless of where they come from, because it's a very narrow area and it's a bottleneck. And from there it then opens up, it fans out, and has many more communications leading on either side. And also the terrain itself is such that a very small force can control a much larger one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And essentially that's what happened in October of 1992, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning chronologically to January of 1993, Major, and paragraph 24 of your summary here. Just before the attacks launched on Busovaca towards the end of January 1993, had there been any movement of Muslim families from that town or municipality into Zenica, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In this period, that is, from New Year's 1993, and even before that -- at first it was less intense, but after the New Year's, the number of people coming from Busovaca increased enormously. And in the Zenica area a large number of Muslims from Busovaca also came. Now, whether they were from the town of Busovaca proper, I don't know, because I didn't contact with them, but they moved to houses where the Serbs were expelled from and where the -- or the houses from which the Croats had left. So I think that these were mostly Muslims who were for the most part from the surrounding villages around Busovaca. This is my opinion. But there could have been some from the town of Busovaca proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, this movement of people from the Busovaca area to Zenica, did this occur before the fighting broke out or after?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you ever hear any of these people contend that they had been forced out of Busovaca as opposed to leaving of their own volition for whatever reason?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I never heard any such story.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Major, about one month before the attack on Busovaca on January 25th of 1993, did you or your intelligence cell receive any information about the amassing of Muslim troops in the area, or did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, before the witness answers, it might be helpful to know what documents he's relied on, I think, for this sort of material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, you can ask him about it in cross-examination. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can answer the question, Major.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Before the attack of 25 January 1993, my service operated in such a way that I received information from not only the Zenica area, but from all other areas. Based on the work of my subordinates and certain things I learned myself, that the Muslim side, the Muslim forces, were grouping in Biljesevo and Kacuni, which is in Busovaca. Obviously, we followed the development of the situation and asked the Muslim side why -- what this meant, because this was very close to Busovaca. Their answers to my questions was that they were amassing reserve forces for potentially enforcement at Visoko against the Bosnian Serbs. But I can say that I had a subordinate officer at the time in the 3rd Battalion of the brigade, and I sent him to the Lasva area, that is, to Biljesevo, more precisely. I think at that time the 333rd Mountain Brigade and 305th Brigades were -- the 333rd was in Kacuni and 305th in Biljesevo. So there was a grouping of forces in my area, and my subordinate officer could not see much. He spent about three days in the area in the field, but he couldn't see much, because the Muslim forces had set up checkpoints and you couldn't reach the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just interrupt you. The soldier or the officer who you sent off to do this reconnoitring work was a man by the name of Ivica Budic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And also the explanation that you described given to you by forces of the ABiH regarding the troop accumulations in the Kacuni and Biljesevo area, were these explanations given to you or to someone else?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, in the context which we had in the field at the time, I could contact with officers from the Territorial Defence and I could even come to the ABiH command. So these answers were given to me, at my insistence, by Mr. Jasmin Saric, because I went to him to look for answers, so he gave me such explanations. And there was another gentleman. I cannot recall his name right now. But the two of them gave me such answers, as well as Mr. Kulovic, who was one of the commanders, Steel Works Battalion. They said that this was the preparation of ABiH forces for the final breakthrough from Visoko to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So these weren't deductions that you were making from documents, these were face-to-face explanations given to you by high-ranking ABiH officers; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. I believe, sir, that you have no first-hand knowledge of the occurrences or the murders that were committed in the villages of Dusina, Miletici, Maljine, Cukle, and other places such as that. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Right, I have no first-hand knowledge. But I have to distinguish between the massacres in Dusina, which took place in early 1993, and Maljine, Cukle, and others happened later, from April to June 1993. So these two things need to be separated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever write any letters to UNPROFOR units concerning these atrocities?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. At that time, I was already a liaison officer with UNPROFOR in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, and a number of such letters, requests, were produced in that context, to investigate those crimes, to try to move the bodies to our cemeteries. I sent a number of such letters to BritBat, but unfortunately we never received any positive responses, except on one occasion Mr. Stavros Kynigopoulos, who I believe worked in the Zenica office, attempted to reach Maljine, where some 43 Croats had been executed. But the Mujahedin forces in the area simply did not allow him to approach and see what had happened there. And then on his return, he told me that he could not get through and see what had happened. And the British forces which were in the area at the time also could do nothing about that at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me move on to your experiences in April 1993, sir. Is it correct that the ABiH attacked -- well, actually I think you've already said this. You've already said that the ABiH attacked the Croats, the Croat inhabitants of Zenica, and the HVO on April the 17th, 1993. Is it also true that a large part of the two Zenica-based brigades, the Jure Francetic Brigade and the Zenicka Brigade, surrendered after a brief period of fighting with the ABiH troops in that city?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, what you said is true. However, before 17 April something else happened which was preparation for the open Muslim attack against Croats, that is, the HVO forces in Zenica. At the time, the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade was abducted, that is, kidnapped, near his command post, and his escorts were brutally murdered. Thousands of bullets were shot into them by unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, unless the Court wishes to hear about this, we actually have Brigadier Totic as one of this week's witnesses. So in the interest of time, we're going to hear about that from someone who was actually involved in the incident, Major, so let's just move on a little bit. Could you tell the Court, in your own words, basically what happened to the remnants of the two brigades and the civilians in the Zenica area after this successful ABiH attack upon the city?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, after the attack of 17 April, about 3.000 HVO soldiers, and even Croat civilians, gathered in Cajdras near Zenica and surrendered to the ABiH, that is, the Muslim forces. That is, there were not just local ABiH forces, there were many others there. Some of them were released to their homes after they had turned in their weapons, and a number of HVO members were taken to the KP Dom or the correctional centre and some to the music school detention facilities. A large number were taken to the Zenica correctional facility, and among them were both civilians and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe your brother was amongst the people captured by the ABiH forces. Could you just, in two or three minutes, tell the Court what happened to him, Major Gelic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: My brother was not imprisoned immediately upon the fall of Zenica. He was taken in several days later. He was interrogated, then released, and forcibly remanded into -- and mobilised and forced to fight against the Croats. After he had spent a certain period of time in some units in Zenica, he was transferred to Kruscica, near Vitez, where he was forced to dig trenches and dugouts where there were no Muslim forces, to burn fires -- so that he would be exposed. And he was forced to live like an animal. I tried to contact him through the Red Cross, but at the time, this was not viable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's one piece of testimony that you gave which was not transcribed particularly clearly, Major. You said that when your brother went to Kruscica, he would be exposed to something. Could you just elaborate upon that in two or three words, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen. This is mistreatment that no normal person should be exposed to. One can survive, but under what circumstances is something else, because such mistreatment, such humiliation which he was subjected to, are not for an animal, let alone for a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, was he or any of his fellow captives used as human shields by the Muslim forces in the Kruscica area?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to talk about things that I am not certain about. But for him, I know for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was he in the military? Was he a soldier before he was captured and forced to do all of these things?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, he was not a soldier at all. First of all, he is partially disabled. He was before he was captured.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You also give an example of some Croat civilians being murdered in your statement. Is it correct that three men were burned to death in a house in Bilivode, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I had such information myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And turning to the last subject I'd like to cover just before the break, with the Court's permission, paragraph 29 of your outline. As a military man, Major, could you give the Court your assessment of the capability that the HVO in Central Bosnia had to mount offensive operations in April of 1993 and thereafter?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As far as HVO forces after April 1993, the forces which were available in the Lasva Valley at the time, they were not prepared nor were they in a position to conduct any offensive operations, simply because they did not have enough ammunition or weapons for any major military operation, and one knows what one needs. But as far as local operations are concerned, there were some in order to consolidate the situation in the Lasva River Valley. But as far as any major offensive operation is concerned, none was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for planning purposes, I would estimate I have another, as you can see from the outline, perhaps 40 minutes of questions for the Major. This might be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, very well. We'll adjourn now for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major Gelic, we've reached paragraph 30 of the summary, and I'd like to turn to the Convoy of Joy incident, about which the Court has heard much evidence. As far as the HVO understood it, could you just let the Court know what route this convoy was going to take in June of 1993, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The Convoy of Joy, as they called it that or, rather, the Tuzla convoy, according to the information I received from the British Battalion, was to go from Novi Travnik to Vilenica, to the town of Travnik, and then on whether either through Guca Gora to Zenica or by Travnik, the Lasva Valley, and then again on to Zenica. However, the information that we had in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that is, until the very day when the convoy arrived, that was the information. And then we were informed that it had changed, the itinerary, and that from Novi Travnik, it went directly through Novi Travnik, Bucici, Ovnak, Nova Bila, and then on via Vitez and on to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was this routing a surprise to the HVO or not, the routing that the convoy actually took as opposed to the routing that you were informed it was going to take?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, at the time, we were not only caught by surprise when we heard of the new route, because it was planned for it to go through the Muslim territory, and in addition to that surprise, that is, the new route, at that time we were in a major predicament, because at that time a very fierce and very forceful Muslim offensive was under way at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The Court has already heard significant evidence about this offensive. It's correct, is it not, that approximately 20.000 Bosnian Croat refugees and displaced persons resulted from the Muslim offensive, military offensive, in early June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. During that offensive, the town of Travnik fell or, rather, the Croats from Travnik had to leave the town. And the remaining Croats -- the remaining Zenica Croats who were in the area of Ovnak, which is a part of the Travnik municipality adjoining the Zenica municipality, Guca Gora, Maljine, Brajkovici, Cukle, all the Croats who lived in that area were driven out by the Muslims, so that about 20.000 expelled civilians and soldiers were in the Lasva Valley at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is it also correct, sir, that immediately before the convoy was stopped, eight small children in the town of Vitez had been killed as a result of an artillery shell landing in their playground, a shell fired from ABiH positions?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. Right before the convoy arrived, children were playing basketball or something else, on a swing, and then that Muslim shell hit that spot and killed -- blew to pieces those children. All those eight children died then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, Major, were you actually in the Vitez area at the time of this convoy incident on June 10th and 11th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The position has been taken in this case that the apprehension of this convoy was a carefully planned move on the part of the HVO and that Mr. Kordic had some role in the planning of that -- of the stoppage of the convoy. From your perspective as a soldier and a member of the headquarters of the HVO, could you give us your best recollection of exactly what happened to this convoy in the second week of June of 1993, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, this thesis that is being placed is not true. There was no plan for that convoy. I already said so. To begin with, we did not really know about the convoy much in advance. Perhaps two or three days before it was due we learned about its existence. And basically we never even gave the convoy a thought, because there were much more important things to think about. Front lines were falling, Croats were being expelled, and one had to deal with all that. So we never really gave much thought to the convoy, let alone planned how to stop it, or think about stopping it. And as to Mr. Kordic planning some stopping of this convoy or anything else, this has nothing to do with the convoy. Such claims are completely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Before your recent involvement in this case in the last couple of months or so, Major, have you ever heard anyone make the contention that Mr. Kordic was somehow involved in the planning of the stoppage of this convoy in any way?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. I never heard such a claim. As you yourself said, I heard this a short time before you called me to come here to testify, so it must be a month or so ago. Otherwise there was no story of that kind in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who actually stopped the convoy, as far as you could see, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, basically I could not see who it was who really stopped the convoy in the area of Travnik. According to the information that I received, and it was from the liaison officer of the British Battalion that I received my information, the convoy was intercepted somewhere in the area of Novi Travnik by civilians, and as such it was broken into pieces, that is, into several parts, and then it continued its journey. And when I started off with the liaison officer of the British Battalion, I was also stopped around Bila, Stara Bila. Stara Bila, that is what I am referring to, where there were three bodies by the lorry. And we also could not get through because of the civilians who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What was your understanding of Mr. Kordic's role in regard to this convoy incident, if any?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, I already said it. Mr. Kordic had absolutely nothing to do with the convoy. However, in view of the reputation he enjoyed, and the British Battalion knew about that, and the European Monitoring Mission, which in a manner of speaking supervised and escorted their security, Captain Perry, as we called him, in that area, I think his name was Clifford, he transmitted the message from his commander, and from the ECMM he requested that somebody with enough authority, and that actually meant Colonel Blaskic, should come to their base, or rather close to their base, to a house, where they could meet, where they could have a brief meeting, at which they would try to once again organise their convoy and send it in the direction in which it was supposed to go. And then the BritBat liaison officer also asked us to look for Mr. Kordic, to ask Mr. Kordic to come to the meeting, because they thought that he was a very prestigious person, that he enjoyed great authority among the civilians in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You referred to a liaison officer and said that you thought his name may have been Clifford. Let me suggest to you, sir, or just mention to you a name and see if this jogs your memory: Captain Lee Whitworth.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Whitworth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Is this the person who you refer to as Captain Perry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think it's better if the witness gives the evidence rather than counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was Captain Perry, Major Gelic, as far as you understood? Was that his real name or was that a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: That's how he introduced himself to us. I believe it was his nickname. And later on I did learn, yes, his real name, and that was Lee Whitworth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me just spring forward. You could, Major, if asked questions about the Muslim offensives against Krizancevo Selo just before Christmas of 1993 and against Santici and Buhine Kuce in January of 1994, if asked questions about those offensives, you could answer them; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Turning to the next subject, paragraph 34 of your summary, you've already described, sir, that you fulfilled liaison officer functions from the middle of May, or approximately the middle of May 1993, until the end of the civil war in March of 1994 with the Central Bosnia Operative Zone headquarters. Could you just let the Court know the kinds of questions that you were asked by representatives of the International Community inquiring about the political structure of the HZ HB and the HR HB?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, it looked a bit odd, all those questions they asked, or the meetings, which were practically a daily occurrence, either with the military side or the ECMM. When I say "military," I mean UNPROFOR forces which were there. The ECMM, UNHCR, or the Red Cross, of all those organisations, I really was baffled why most of these discussions bore upon the political situation in Central Bosnia. Should I say some 60 per cent of the questions related to the political situation rather than the military situation. That is, those were not the questions for which -- which fell within my field of operation. They had to do with something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: When the question of the political situation or the political hierarchy arose, what did you inform these representatives of the International Community that they should do in order to find out the answers to the questions they were asking you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, basically to all those questions, because I really did not know the answers to these questions, what was going on in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and then the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, who held which political office, I simply did not have adequate information. Perhaps I did have some information, but very little, so that all those political questions they were asking -- that were asked by international representatives basically came down to the fact that other politicians who lived there and worked there, and could they go to them to seek additional information. And also they had press conferences which took place on Tuesdays, mostly, and they could also ask those supplementary questions there at those press conferences. And there were also local politicians who also held their press conferences, and simply those questions they were asking me about politics should have been asked -- they should have been addressed to those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just to summarise that position, would it be fair to say that you were obviously a man with a military background and you knew about military things, but if questions arose regarding the political situation, you directed the interrogators to the politicians themselves or to their press conferences at which those questions could be addressed and answered?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, is it also right, sir, looking at paragraph 37 of your outline, that the military in the Vitez/Busovaca area, the HVO military itself, held regular press conferences separate and distinct from the Tuesday press conferences that were held by the political figures that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You see, as liaison officer, my task was similar. That is, Commander Colonel Tihomir Blaskic issued such an order to us who were in the special department which had to do with public relations, with journalists, and the International Community, to organise military press conferences which were held on a weekly basis; not on a particular day of the week, but we usually held them on Thursdays. And they were taking place in the area of Bila or, rather, in the immediate vicinity of the British Battalion, and all the world TV companies and other media were there. And the military therefore had their separate military briefings, which did not have anything to do with other briefings held in Travnik, or Busovaca, or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Is it fair to say that the person who introduced or opened these military press conferences was a man by the name of Marko Prskalo?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, he started it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And then other persons such as Mr. Saric, different from Jasmin Saric, obviously, and Ms. Topic would cover other items during those press conferences; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Basically, I worked more with Mr. Saric and Miss Topic. She was a "Miss" then. And I worked more with them than Mr. Prskalo, because Mr. Prskalo was there before I came to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning to paragraph 38 of your outline, two matters. A contention has been made in this case that Mr. Kordic once appeared on a television programme shortly after the roadblock at Ahmici in October of 1992 and made certain threats to do things to Ahmici and its residents. I believe the contention has been made that he threatened to raze Ahmici to the ground. Had you ever heard that story before in all of your time in the HVO in the Central Bosnia area, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I had never heard that before, before I came here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There's another contention made by one witness, I think, that shortly or the day before the fighting broke out in Central Bosnia in April the 16th, 1993, Mr. Kordic supposedly appeared on a television programme, for which we do not have a videotape, stating that his soldiers were ready and just awaiting orders of some sort. Have you ever heard that any such TV appearance was made by Mr. Kordic, sir, at any time during your tenure in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think it was on the 16th of April that Mr. Kordic did appear on television or, rather, at that press conference which they had organised on the occasion of the abduction of the commander of the Jure Francetic Brigade, Zivko Totic, and I watched it. I believe it took place in the morning, but the system was such that in Zenica, we could watch it only in the afternoon. But it had to do with the abduction of Mr. Zivko Totic, and nothing else was mentioned then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: This television programme that you saw, sir, was that aired on the same day that Commander Totic was abducted and his guards killed, or the day after, or can't you remember?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think it was the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, one other matter I would like to cover with you is an allegation that's been made in this case to the effect that the HVO, within its military organisation, had the functional equivalent of political commissars or political officers, also known as zampolits, of the type associated with the armed forces of the former Soviet Union. Is that correct, sir, is it true? Is there any substance to that theory or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, such allegations are basically untrue. I know that there's been talk about such things, but the HVO never had any political officers who would be responsible for that in the HVO, and the law on the armed forces forbids officers to engage in politics or deal with political matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Kordic ever serve as a political commissar of the HVO in any fashion, as far as you're aware, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Turning very briefly to three items that conclude your testimony, Major, I'd like to address your memory, if I can, to July the 5th of 1993, when a lady by the name of Dobrila Kolaba, an UNPROFOR interpreter, was shot dead at the BritBat compound in Bila. Did the HVO perform any investigation into the killing of Ms. Kolaba on that day, and if so, could you just tell the Court, in your own words, the circumstances under which such an investigation occurred and what your involvement was, if any, in it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Quite true, as you said, Dobrila Kolaba was killed on the 5th of July, 1993, and at the request of the UNPROFOR British Battalion, which was then quartering at the compound at Divjak, they requested that an investigation be conducted. I must say that the HVO highly appreciated Ms. Dobrila as an interpreter there. We had a very high opinion of her as a correct interpreter, and we were very sorry when that happened. Colonel Blaskic then also made a point of requesting an investigation about the incident. And since I was a liaison officer at the time, I played the role of a -- a coordinating role between the HVO investigating team and the British army which was there; that is, I was a kind of coordinator or liaison officer as a go-between in this investigation. Unfortunately, we never managed to bring that investigation to an end. That is, we could not arrive at the exact evidence on that thing. There were several possibilities, but the most important thing is that we could not see Ms. Dobrila's body because the British officers had already -- that place -- or her body, they had already taken away her body from the place where she had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you able to reach any conclusions about whether Ms. Kolaba was killed by an individually-targeted shot, or by a burst of gunfire, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, look, from what one could see on the house, that is, bullet marks, one could hardly say that she was killed by a bullet, by one bullet. There could have been several short bursts of fire or perhaps one longer burst of fire, and then one of them hit Ms. Dobrila. That is, according to what we could see on the facade on the front side of the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Let me turn to the next subject, sir, which was the shooting of the UNHCR driver in Stari Vitez on August the 14th, 1993. Does the name Boris Zevracic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: "Boris", yes. "Zevracic", I am not so sure about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know the unfortunate person who was shot on in armoured vehicle that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew that person even from before the war, because he lived in Zenica, in the same neighbourhood with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether the HVO performed any investigation into the circumstances of this gentleman's death, and if so, what your role in it was, if any?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, again the investigation of that murder was conducted, but because of the site at which it happened, we simply had no access to the scene. And the truck in which they worked had immediately been taken to the British Battalion compound, and the investigation could not be performed in a proper manner. Moreover, the evidence which existed, one of the key exhibits would be the bullet which hit the driver, I know that Captain Perry then told me and showed me the bullet, and there were the words "Steel Works Zenica", "Zeljezara Zenica", on it. And then I said that we simply could not have such a bullet, nor could we make a bullet with that particular mark, and I asked them to give that bullet to our investigating team. But from what I can remember, there was never again even a discussion about that murder or about that incident, so that the investigation could not be brought to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
