utterances.text: All right. The last subject I would like to address with you, Major, is the subject of the use of helicopters by certain persons. To your knowledge, did Colonel Blaskic ever use a helicopter at any time in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How many times?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I remember one occasion towards the end of 1993. He was in a helicopter to go to Herzegovina. Whether he also used it before that, I can't say that, because I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Other than UNPROFOR helicopters, sir, did you ever hear of political figures like Mr. Kordic or others ever using military helicopters belonging to the HVO or at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know of any such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of an occasion when shortly before -- actually, immediately before the foundation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in August of 1993, about 28 political figures from a number of municipalities in Central Bosnia were taken to Kiseljak and then flown in UNPROFOR helicopters from Kiseljak to Medjugorje, where the convention to consider the establishment of the HR HB was being held?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that. It is, yes, true, twenty-eight persons from Central Bosnia. They were all politicians, and I believe Mr. Dario Kordic was one of them. Yes, that was August 1993. UNPROFOR vehicles took them from Vitez to Kiseljak, and then I think they proceeded by helicopter. I believe it was an UNPROFOR helicopter. They were taken further on to their destination. I don't really know which one it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was that the only time that you ever heard, in your entire time with the HVO, of Mr. Kordic actually using an UNPROFOR helicopter, or not using but being transported in an UNPROFOR helicopter?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Major, thank you very much. That concludes my examination. If you'll wait, you may be asked some questions by Mr. Cerkez' counsel and then by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gelic. We met. My name is Bozidar Kovacic, with Mr. Mikulicic. We represent Mr. Cerkez in these proceedings. I have only a very few questions for you just in the way of clarification of certain things that you stated. The first topic that I want to address is the Convoy of Joy that you have spoken about. This is June of 1993. Would you agree that the convoy was stopped by people for the first time in the territory of Novi Travnik and on several occasions before it even reached the territory of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding the incidents relating to the convoy, also to place when the convoy reached Nova Bila, that is, Bila, when it entered Travnik, there were further incidents and civilians were stopping the convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In addition, in the territory of Vitez municipality, due to all these activities, and you mentioned some of those, an attempt was made to consolidate the convoy and allow it further passage; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gelic, is it correct that one of the spots where this gathering of convoy was attempted was near Mosunj?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the second was near the Vitezit factory, that is, the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And throughout that day, together with Lee Whitworth, whom you mentioned, you were engaged in these activities?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Not only one day; this took two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were called from Vitez when they said that somebody from the Operative Zone, as Blaskic's representatives, should be there to try to resolve the problems with the convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, Officer Perry came with his Warrior, and we went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When did he pick you up?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Between the Hotel Vitez and the post office.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Immediately before this meeting with Whitworth, were you in the post office building?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the post office building, did you see Mario Cerkez was present there, who is present here?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I saw both him and his two escorts who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And immediately after you set out with Whitworth near the Impregnacija company, which is on the main road near Bila, there was again a place -- a location where the civilians had blocked the convoy?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How much later was that after you had seen Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: About an hour and a half later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the Impregnacija location, did you see Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did Lee Whitworth say that he saw him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In this melee, did you see any HVO officers?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I only saw one HVO officer, who was in front of the civilians, and by the time we went back, that is, those 100, 200 meters, by the time we approached, he had left the scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this person trying to make some order among these civilians?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know what he was doing there. I don't know if he was just passing there, but he had nothing to do with the civilians who were gathered there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. In that regard, we heard evidence here, and it was said that in this context efforts to resolve the situation. But let me ask you the question in another way. Did you know a person by the name of Anto Breljas?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this person a member of the Vitezovi unit?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did he perform an IPD officer function at any time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this Breljas, did you meet him at any time while you were visiting and touring and trying to resolve the situation about the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But do you know that Breljas at any time would have figured as an interpreter to UNPROFOR or to Whitworth?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. That would not have been possible, because all British officers had with them their own interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on to another topic. You talked about 1992 and how the HVO was established and the problems concerning that organisation. You said that the HVO was organised on the territorial principle. Does that mean that the HVO was always linked to the municipality from where it drew its manpower?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. The territorial principle was the basis of organisation, and it was always in a municipality where it was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was the civilian authorities who -- the HVO civilian authorities which were organising these units?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it was the civilian branch of the HVO which was the organiser of this defence, that is, of this organisation, of this military organisation?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, that was the usual way, from the civilian arm of the HVO, the HVO government, and according to the principles and agreements, these military structures were set up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the municipalities, at least in the majority of municipalities where the HVO was present in Central Bosnia, there were bodies which were known as the HVO staffs, and they were in charge of the defence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And these were the key administrative bodies that engaged in the defence matters?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that from July 1992, the brigades were starting to be established, and you gave us the example of the Zenica case. But is it true that in a number of Central Bosnia municipalities, brigades were not established until later that year, late fall and on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: All brigades were officially established in December 1992. But this is a process. This cannot be said to be -- to have been possible to establish in a day. So it took months before all these brigades were formed and the Central Bosnia Operative Zone was in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gelic, can you tell us, given that you were in Travnik at the time, but do you know that in Novi Travnik, from December 1992, the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade existed?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that that was a intermunicipal brigade; that is, Novi Travnik and Vitez municipalities both contributed to it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with it, but I know that it had members from both municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that later in 1993, that is, in the middle of 1993, the Vitez Brigade was established in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As you knew the situation and the circumstances, could you give us even the roughest of estimates? Under normal circumstances, how much time would it take for a brigade to be established?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In my previous answer, I said that it takes months. It's not a month or two. In order to have a quality organisation, you need five to six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can I understand from what you just said that when an order was formally issued to establish the Vitez Brigade in the middle of March, that it could not have been established as a reasonable organisation for about five to six months?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been a reasonable amount of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gelic, in the period between December 1992 up to April 1993, do you know whether -- there were no major conflicts between the two sides, the ABiH or Territorial Defence in the HVO; that is, in the territory of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that, in fact, after the October conflict in Travnik, the territory of Novi Travnik, until April 1993, the status quo remained?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the status quo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the status quo was a consequence of an agreement of the two sides, on the one hand and on the other hand, of a factual division of town?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think that it was a factual division of town by the two sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in spite of this, the two sides still held a joint defence line against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, a defence line was held against the Serbs, but each side had its own sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean its own sector of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question. You said that in early 1993, or maybe even late 1992, the 305th ABiH came to Biljesevo. Do you know whether this brigade came to this area after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was a brigade from Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Now, this 305th Brigade which arrived in the Vitez pocket was not the only unit which arrived there after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is not the only unit which arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell, in military sense, that after the fall of Jajce, the balance of forces was further disrupted against the HVO because of the influx of all the units that came after the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Even before the fall of Jajce a large number of refugees came from Western Bosnia. They had been driven out by the Serbs. And the ABiH organised these people. They organised them into new brigades. And especially after the fall of Jajce into Serbian hands, this ratio was even more skewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I understand. In this process of migration, did the 17th Krajina Brigade also arrive there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Into the Vitez pocket?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the 17th Krajina Brigade had a reputation of being an aggressive and fairly radical unit?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. As I previously stated when I talked -- when I referred to my brother, the 17th Krajina Brigade kept a part of their forces in the Kruscica area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And is it true that those parts of the 17th Krajina Brigade in Kruscica, in many of its activities and through their behaviour, spread significant fear among the civilians in the area and also among the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: They had two brigades: the 7th Muslim Brigade and the 17th Krajina Brigade, who, among the civilians, if such civilians remained under the control of the ABiH, lived in fear of them, lived in fear of their passing through or being in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the local commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade was Fikret Cuskic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, for a time, yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was he known as somebody who engaged in propaganda and misinformation?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Gelic, I think you came here a couple of weeks ago last Friday and you were expecting to give evidence then, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: That was the plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had your summary been prepared by then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In a way, I had given a statement then, but I have worked on a summary on several occasions, including several days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to the work you may have had to do on it in a minute, but it's right that you've also discussed the evidence you were going to answer to Mr. Cerkez's counsel with his counsel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. He asked me several questions regarding the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the usher could very kindly move the ELMO so that I can see the witness and he can see me if he wishes to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we also have the microphone closer to the Prosecutor turned on for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. The other microphone on the witness's side, please. Can you turn it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One or two things aren't clear from your evidence, but I hope to make them clear. Where were you on the 16th of April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that you've been in Zenica from 1992 through to 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I was in Zenica even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. And in Zenica you were mostly involved in intelligence work?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, I was a member of the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what that involved your doing. Did you have an office?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It is a regular thing for every -- for the establishment of any unit to have an intelligence service which is scrutinising the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you have an office?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in your office you had a telephone, and what other communication systems did you have, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I had a fax machine and I also had a computer, not in my office but in the office next door.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The fax machine would communicate with anywhere that the telephone system could reach in Bosnia or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Wherever we had links, this is where we were able to send communications. But this fax machine was not used that much, for both technical and security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You also had mobile telephones?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did others have mobile telephones? If not in Zenica, by the time you got to Vitez, did they have mobile telephones there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I saw the first mobile telephone in the Lasva Valley sometime around 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And by "mobile telephone", I'm not necessarily meaning a modern form of telephone, but some form of hands-free radio telephone that enabled people to communicate over distance. Did you see any of those?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You mean like Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So my mistake, of course, in calling it a mobile telephone. But you had Motorolas right from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Not all of us had it. The signals unit used it most, not other officers; only if they went out into the field someplace. Because the range is very small. The good range is only three kilometers. And the configuration of terrain in Bosnia is such that it does not allow such communications because of the radio waves. They get interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In your office in Zenica, with whom outside Zenica did you regularly communicate?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I had -- in my chain of command I had a superior, that is, an official superior, the person who was in charge of intelligence work --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: -- and so one was reporting to the superior, which was at the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The person at Zenica to whom you reported, what was his name?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Zivko Totic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And in the Central Bosnia Operational Zone, who was that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In the Operative Zone it was Colonel Ivica Zeko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How regularly did you communicate to him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It depended on needs. Twice a day, three times a day. But in principle, a report was sent one in the morning and another one in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So these were written or typed reports?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It depended. Sometimes they were written, sometimes they were oral. Sometimes there was no need for me to write anything down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your reports to Zivko Totic would sometimes be oral, sometimes be written?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, we did have regular morning briefings with the commander of the brigade, and that happened when Zivko Totic was there too. And it would detail the situation as it was. And it included written reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. This pattern of communication, and in particular the pattern of communication to the Central Bosnia Operational Zone continued right up and until the time you moved from Zenica to Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Look, this type of communication was not always -- how shall I put it? -- fully functional. Sometimes there were a lot of holes in this whole chain which had to be plugged, and obviously I did continue to do so when I transferred to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can't at the moment, can you, identify any particular periods of time when there was a gap in communication, for reasons of mechanical breakdown?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Mechanical breakdowns? I cannot recall such instances, but after the fall of the HVO in Zenica, there was a gap of about 15 days. I had to hide in Zenica in order not to be captured by either Mujahedins or the ABiH. I had to hide very well in order to avoid being captured, and at that time obviously the communication was interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what days do you say that was, just to help us, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: This was from 17 April and the following about 15 days, until I crossed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once you were in Vitez and working there -- well, let me start again. You got to Vitez. Did you start working there immediately?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I immediately became an associate for intelligence in the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia. Naturally, one had to recover mentally to simply pull himself back together in order to continue his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Once in Vitez and in post, the process of recording and reporting continued, but now you'd be reporting directly in Vitez and communicating with other stations elsewhere. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Once you were in Vitez, the process of reporting regularly to your superiors there continued?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There would also have been communication with other places, other posts outside Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I could communicate only within Vitez, because everything that we sent went through one packet system. There was no other possibility of communication. Everything went to one centre, to one hub. So my reports went at that time towards Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That's by the packet system for distribution from Mostar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the ultimate destinations of the reporting that you were doing beyond Mostar were where? Which places were you hoping to communicate to if the Mostar system worked? Where else?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Mostar itself, the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You never sent any communications to any other area, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You mean in the command of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Only in HVO, through the HVO, could the reports go to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you keep a diary?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is your diary?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not get the answer.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I know that I had it at home for a while, sometime until '94, and then I think my son used it to learn -- to practice writing in the same notebook. And after that, I really don't know. I can't remember where exactly I left it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In preparing your summary for this Court, have you referred to any documents in order to give the summary that's been provided?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I did not use any documents, simply things that stuck in my memory, and it was on the basis of that that I prepared this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We will come back to what you said about working on your summary. Within the last two weeks, there have been no documents to which you've been able to refer, so over the last two weeks, if you can help us, what bits of memory have come back or what bits of detail have you been able to deal with over the last two weeks that you weren't able to deal with by a fortnight ago?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As for this summary, as such, the only document I saw was the one that the lawyers gave me. But it was in English, so I just didn't really understand it. I couldn't understand it properly, and it concerned an ECMM report. And what I wrote here, I amended it several times; that is, I expanded it here and there. Simply, when one begins to put something on paper, their memories begin to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the document that you prepared a fortnight ago didn't need correcting, even if it needed amplifying; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, no, that is not correct. There were quite a number of things that I added or to quote, simply because I remembered certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who, in the area, did exercise political control, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In what area?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Zenica first.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In Zenica and -- there were two different political areas. The Muslims had their own, and the Croats had their own too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So far as conduct of military matters is concerned, were the military men making the decisions themselves or were they responding to political leadership? Please tell us.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: There is a chain of command in the army, and decisions are taken on that basis; nothing to do with politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So when you were in Zenica, were you aware, one way or another, of any political influence over any decisions that were being made by the military?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen, as far as that is concerned, I wasn't really particularly interested to know what politicians did, because that was their daily work, and our daily work was quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question again, in case you can help us. When in Zenica, were you aware of any political influence over the decisions made by the military?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were in Vitez, were you aware of any political influence over decisions made by the military?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that the military men made all the decisions about the conduct of this war themselves and there was no political input, or is it your position that you simply don't know one way or another because you weren't sufficiently senior in rank to know?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen, the system of command, as I have already explained, is the fundamental manner of functioning of the army, and that is how decisions are taken. Whether there is some link with politics, I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to complete this: For example, in Vitez, did you have a lot of contact with Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: More or less, during morning briefings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And did he never identify any politician taking any part in the decisions that were being made?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe I already answered it already twice, or even thrice, and I always said, "No." So I shall repeat it again: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So from your position, your perspective, it looked as though the war was simply being run by the military completely, start to finish?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What part were the politicians playing at all, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, ask them. I wasn't into politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were there, Major. What part did you see the politicians taking in the conduct of affairs in 1992, 1993, when there was a war on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. Once again, I'm telling you I am a soldier, and these political questions you should ask of politicians, because that is what they deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The man Whitworth, you got on quite well with him, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No reason to doubt his honesty or reliability at the time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You say that, not me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you. You were there. Any reason to doubt his honesty or reliability at the time, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, it depends. I will keep my conclusions to myself. I'd really rather not speak about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is your chance to give me your opinions now, please, because if there's something that shows he's unreliable, I'd like to know.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen, as for the performance of his tasks, he also did as much as he could, considering the situation. Whether all he did was done correctly, I don't know, and it is his superior officer who can judge that. Also, how we saw what they were doing, I can make my judgements. I worked with him, and I know that some of his tasks he indeed performed correctly, and yet there were some questionable moments. Let me put it that way, "moments."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I want you to feel free to tell us what the questionable moments are when they come to your memory. And this is the later part of your testimony rather than the earlier part, but if he says that you were a great facilitator in moving around the territory when you were the liaison officer in Vitez, would you accept that, that you were very useful, you were very helpful, in getting by checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. As for that, not only me, not only I, but the majority of officers and commanders in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone did their best to maintain the best possible cooperation with all international organisations, UNPROFOR included.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you were able to get people by many checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were able to get people, like Whitworth and other members of the International Community, you were able to get them where they wanted to go and to get by checkpoints on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But there were some occasions when even you couldn't do that; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On those occasions, the people at the checkpoints would want some other authority before they would allow even someone like Mr. Whitworth to pass?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: On those occasions, do you accept that sometimes it would be a local brigade commander whose authority would be requested and sometimes it would be a name like Mr. Kordic that would be referred to?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. In all those cases that I was involved with, the responsible person could be the commander in the area, or at worst, one would have to seek authorisation from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're saying there was never any occasion when you heard Kordic's name referred to as the person whose authority was required?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I shall repeat: I sought authority from Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. Were there any occasions at checkpoints where people were not inclined to let you through on your own authority but mentioned Kordic as the person whose authority they would accept?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, it did not happen in my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you [indiscernible] first in Zenica and then in Vitez, or if you were not at the hub, at a sort of hub of the passage of intelligence, weren't you? You were receiving intelligence from others and you were properly communicating intelligence to others?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And when you were in Zenica, were you hearing about -- for the proper interests of your side, were you hearing about things that were happening elsewhere, in Busovaca and in Vitez and so on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I had my area of responsibility as far as intelligence was concerned, and it covered Kakanj, Zenica, up to Travnik, excluding Busovaca, Vitez, Novi Travnik, because they had their brigades and it was their area of responsibility. And as for the exchange of information, we did it once a fortnight or once a week when we would hold our joint meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you did -- where did you hold the joint meetings, by the way?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And at none of those occasions, by meetings or other communication, did you ever hear of Kordic's name being required to free a checkpoint for passage?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen, you are taking me back, with your questions, to go back to the checkpoints, and I'm now talking about meetings. That was prior to 1992 until April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Gelic, don't worry about the questions and where counsel is going. Just answer "Yes" or "No," and we'll get on more quickly and we'll finish your evidence.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Starting now in 1992, the original allocation of arms in Zenica, was that an allocation of arms basically to the Territorial Defence, as it then was?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The first distribution of weapons in Zenica was to be done by the Territorial Defence and the reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it was to those established and lawful bodies that the weapons initially went?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of the Zenica HVO being set up for particular reasons, and I want to be quite sure I understand this. What authority did the local Zenica HVO have for coming into existence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The legal authority, I couldn't answer this because the answer will be too long. But I already said that I was the commander of the Territorial Defence at Broda, and since that group -- that is a legal unit. It could not get the weapons from that same Territorial Defence which had the supreme command of that Territorial Defence in Zenica. And on the basis of what people were asking, that we separate from all of this, that was when we started setting up Croat forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And Broda is a Croat area, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, not purely Croat. It is a mixed area. That is, there were also -- there were all Muslims, Croats, and Serbs lived in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I come back. What authority was there for the establishment of something called the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: To begin with, the HVO had its political authority, political -- you know, the political part which existed there. But in truth, what happened in my case, because I'm talking about my case, people simply refused to be part of the Territorial Defence any longer because that Territorial Defence did not give them any possibility to defend themselves. And that was when we set up Croat defence forces, and then we joined other units which were formed in the territory of Zenica at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, all of this will be recorded in writing somewhere, won't it, because the archives of the local HVO should still exist somewhere?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen. When the HVO fell in Zenica, I do not think that even a trace of all these papers remains. Perhaps somewhere else; I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that a guess or are you telling us, from some evidence, that you believe that the documents were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. I cannot prove that, but what I can do is say that I have not seen those documents since the fall of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have you even looked for them?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're aware that before the HVO in Zenica was established, political moves had been made by Herceg-Bosna to set up the HVO as the supreme defence body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, then I come again. What authority was there? You say it's too long an answer. You obviously know the position. What body enabled you to set up this new military force in Zenica, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: We. There was no legal body. It was the wish of the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And purely by chance, it was called the HVO?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen. It was later on systematised, brought together, organised in a body which was called the HVO. But that organisation of Croats in the beginning was, as I told you, people wanted it; that is, we wanted it. And then subsequently, logically, legal regulations were passed, a law was passed, to make it officially the HVO. The HVO did not exist as of the moment when I said the word "HVO", but I believe that it was on the 8th of April, 1992, that the Croat Defence Council was set up officially. And before that, we had already formed those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so you were aware, certainly by the 8th of April of 1992, that you were part of a military force that was substantially monoethnic. It simply reflected Croat support; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. The HVO was not a monoethnic force, at least insofar as Zenica is concerned. I cannot talk about other places, but that was not the case in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: To what extent do you say there was ethnic representation of non-Croats in Zenica? What percentage, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know. I can tell you about my brigade, the brigade that I was in. We had Serbs in that unit, and there were also several Muslims who joined the Croat Defence Council and who were quite normal soldiers in that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, you said a law was passed for the HVO. Who passed the law?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I do not know who passed that law.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you say in your summary, as I followed it, that it was because of the difficulty with the Muslims, really, and the allocation of weapons that you had to set up the HVO. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Could you help me, please? Tell me, which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you not remember, Major Gelic? Do you need to look at the summary to tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, listen. You are asking me about things which -- you are talking about the HVO, and this paragraph speaks of the Territorial Defence. I was the commander of the Territorial Defence in a locality called Broda, near Zenica, and in that same unit of Territorial Defence, the Croats and the Muslims were together. And we could not get the weapons from that same Territorial Defence, that is, the higher-level Territorial Defence, because -- and because of that, people at Broda decided not to participate in the Territorial again because the Muslim side would not allow us to have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, the Muslim side decided not to let you have any weapons? Are you telling us, just so we've got the picture, that you nevertheless had Muslims in your group, which became the HVO, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But you can't tell us how many?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I can't give you the exact number. Well, it wasn't a very high percentage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And just maybe this is a convenient place to break, but can you help us by telling us where, if other than in Zenica, there would be any documents going to reflect the creation of the HVO in Zenica in the way you've described? Can you tell us where we can find any documents about that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that. I don't know where they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I'm not going to take matters any further, it having not been the subject of earlier notice and there being no documents that I could find. I don't know if that would be a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice, it would be. How long do you anticipate you'll be?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: An hour, but I'll do it as quickly as I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, if you would, so we can get through these witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I inquire whether the Prosecution intends to be through by this afternoon, because we do have another witness lined up. And if obviously Major Gelic is going to take the whole afternoon, we would like to release the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope so, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have the witness here just in case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Gelic, we're going to adjourn now until half past 2.00. During that adjournment, please don't speak to anybody about your evidence, and of course don't let anybody speak to you about it. That does include the members of the Defence teams. Half past 2.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before we leave May 1992, Major Gelic, would you help us, please, with this. Filip Filipovic, did you have much to do with him?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In that period, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his job then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of him losing the position of commanding officer generally and being substituted by someone else?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As I said, in respect of Mr. Filipovic, I don't know as regards that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you had come from the Territorial Defence and had joined an HVO unit. He was in charge of the HVO generally. Weren't you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't know that Mr. Filipovic was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware at that time, please, of any plan involving General Merdan to set up a joint command headed by Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The period that is until May 1992, I am not aware of any plan that Mr. Filipovic would make any joint staffs or command structures with Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any such plan at any stage?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Not as regards Mr. Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that there was such a plan and that it was Dario Kordic who stood in the way of the plan getting off the ground. Does that fit with your memory at all?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I have stated that in late 1991 until April 1992, I was the commander of the Territorial Defence at Broda and that in that capacity I spoke with officials in Zenica TO about building a joint command armed force. This is what we talked about. And we talked about the arming of the population, but this didn't take place. And I don't know of any other plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then you speak of the Muslims rounding up criminals in May of 1992. You accept, I think, from what you've told us, that there was a genuine effort by them to round up criminals; yes?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. I believe I said that this was an attempt to provoke an incident with Croats who were in that building -- actually, in the building across, where supposedly the arrest of those criminals was under way. Because as I'm aware, only one of these criminals was ever arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But the suggestion that this was trying to stimulate an armed response is mere speculation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It's not speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You don't have any piece of hard evidence to go on for the suggestion that you've made?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The only firm evidence is myself, because I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All you saw was an attempt to round up criminals?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I saw a different picture. This attempted arrest of criminals seemed to me -- I believe that I know how an arrest is to take place. It is not done by blocking roads and streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: About this time, Kordic was appearing on Radio Zenica from time to time, wasn't he? Did you see those appearances?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was on only one occasion that I heard Mr. Kordic. It was something to do with negotiations surrounding the takeover of the barracks in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So what was this politician doing, discussing on television the takeover of barracks, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what he did. I believe that he was involved in some negotiations with the commander of Zenica barracks and some other people who were there. I don't know exactly who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's a military activity, isn't it, the takeover of a barracks? It's not a political activity?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: This was not a takeover of the barracks. I'm not talking about the takeover; I'm talking about the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Negotiations to take them over, and that's different, is it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your wife's removal from the apartment, you weren't there yourself at the time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I personally was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you living in that apartment at that time, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you tell us who you say it was evicted her, give us the name?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know the name, because she herself did not know the name, but this was the MOS police who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was any complaint registered about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In writing?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So tell us, please, where we can find it, and we'll go and look for it.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe that it's in the 3rd Corps in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The documents that registered complaint, did you keep a copy yourself?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I had them until April of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You speak of an expulsion of Croats in June of 1992 in Zenica, by which time you were the chief of HVO intelligence there. So, please, who was the first Croat expelled, and by whom?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe that the family was Kovacevic from Bistricak, and they were expelled by members of the Mujahedin forces who, together with the local Muslims, took them to a training camp. This is how they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And any record of this? Where will we find a record of this?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: About these expelled families or, that is, this expelled family?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Such a document should be in the International Red Cross archives, because I think that the case was reported to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But kept anywhere else? Your local HVO would have kept a record of it, presumably?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: We only had -- I myself had an official report. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that's no longer in existence or you don't know?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As I said, from April 1993, I -- since April 1993, I never saw a single document which I used to have in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By October 1992, you had been in your post for some four months, and as I understand it, you were communicating most with which other areas; Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I already said the zone of responsibility of my brigade was Kakanj, Zenica, up to Novi Travnik and up to Vares. But as I said, we had meetings in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So ceasefires agreed, for example, in Novi Travnik would be matters in which you, as an intelligence officer, would have an interest?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember an incident where Colonel Stewart, on the 20th of October of 1992, dealt with a ceasefire in Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. At that time, I did not know this gentleman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was the colonel in charge of Cheshires, who were doing their six-month tour of duty. Does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I only heard his name, but I never worked with him and I never had an opportunity to meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But what I want to know is this: A ceasefire, Major, is a military activity, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And such a military activity in Novi Travnik would have come to your attention in some way and at some stage, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, of course we received information by military means about the ceasefire.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why any politician should be involved in negotiating a ceasefire in October 1992 at Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe that in most of these matters, even what concerns military, it is the politicians who first negotiate, and only later soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If that be right, then what is it that the politicians are doing with the soldiers, if they are not controlling them, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: What the politicians do with soldiers, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll ask the question in another way. For a politician to be able to negotiate a ceasefire means that the politician is able to command the soldiers; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: In your interpretation, it may be so. But in our military system, it is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then can you explain what your answer two answers ago meant when you said this: "I believe that in most of these matters, even what concerns military, it is the politicians who first negotiate, and only later the soldiers"? What is it that politicians are able to do first if it doesn't necessarily involve the ability to command the soldiers? What is it they are able to do, please, Major?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The politicians probably agree on certain things at that political level. This is my assumption. And then down the chain of command, I don't know, there may be some extended arm and it is passed down. But this is only my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So "down the chain of command" means from the politicians to the soldiers. It's quite simple, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: When referring to 1992, that wasn't that simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you were there receiving and sending messages, as you have confirmed to us. Do you accept that on the 20th of October of 1992, as Colonel Stewart has told us, a politician, Dario Kordic, was in a position to negotiate a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Listen, Counsel. Perhaps you can ask Colonel Stewart of that. I was not in a situation to be there and to talk to them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were on the ground. You're telling us that Kordic had no military responsibility. Colonel Stewart has already given his evidence, and I want you to tell us, please, from your experiences, which is why you're here, Major, do you accept that at that time Kordic was in a position to negotiate the terms of a ceasefire agreement?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: From the political side, probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next question: Because you were sending and receiving information, including information about Novi Travnik, did you or did you not know that Kordic was doing such things as negotiating ceasefires?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I will repeat it one more time. My zone of responsibility was Zenica, and this information came from Travnik and Novi Travnik. I could only receive information about the ceasefire or something of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you receive information that Kordic had negotiated the ceasefire, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There would be no reason that you can think of to keep such details from you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: There would be no reason to hide such details from me, there was no reason for that, but I have to remind you that time flew by in those days and events succeeded each other very quickly, and one would be replaced by another one the next moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the Registry could just dig out Exhibit 243, please. While we're coming to that in just a minute, a word or two about Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position about Jajce is this, isn't it: At the time, it had a broadly even distribution of Croats and Muslims, with the Serbs in the minority; correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know the prewar population structure of Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What you can confirm is that when Jajce fell, as it in due course did to the Serbs, it wasn't associated with any bloodbath or killings or anything of that sort; it just fell?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There wasn't any bloodbath, any major or significant losses of life associated with the fall of Jajce, I'm suggesting to you.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know if -- in your place, I wouldn't be so sure. There were a lot of casualties in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You certainly can't point to any known or publicised loss of life associated with the fall of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I believe that even monuments have been erected to commemorate that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were in intelligence, therefore receiving intelligence from various sources. Is it the case that Jajce was subject to an agreement between the Croats and the Serbs, that it should pass to the Serb hands?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Sir, I went to Jajce on three occasions with my unit, and I believe that should -- that speaks volumes about the so-called agreements. Why would I be taking my men to Jajce to be killed if there was any agreement available?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's look at this next exhibit. You're saying it's a genuine battle involving and requiring military input.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Shall we look at the next exhibit, Exhibit 243, please, the original for the witness. Can I have -- if you could put the English version. It will be the last page of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, this may not be a document you've seen recently, or at all. First of all, do you recollect seeing it at all, ever?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I never saw this document, and I also believe that this document has not been signed either.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you'd like to look, nevertheless, at the last page, what is paragraph 10, you'll see a paragraph that reads, and I'll read it slowly: "While defence operations are being conducted, the vice-president of the HZ HB, Dario Kordic, and I, are in Novi Travnik, continuously leading the military operations, with deep knowledge of the situation, by keeping all forces under control. Colonel Filipovic is also here and the Novi Travnik HVO HQ." The names at the foot of that are Blaskic and Kordic, and there is a handwritten received note dated the 27th of October of 1992. Now, this is at Novi Travnik. This isn't at Jajce. But just tell us: Do you still maintain that Kordic had no military involvement of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still maintain this. But first of all, I've never seen this document before, and to me, this document is not a valid one, because I don't see any signatures or a stamp on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, I want you to look at a video, moving on from the first Ahmici incident, for reasons of speed, to the end of the year. I want you to look at a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give me one minute, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The position, Your Honour, is that there's a short video for which we have a transcript available. The present quality of the video is apparently appalling, although it may be capable of being improved, but not today. There are three courts sitting today and the technical staff are fully stretched. I haven't even seen it yet myself, but I'm informed how bad it is. What I'd like to do, just for identification purposes, is to play the first small passage so that we can know what the video is. It can, I gather, be corrected, possibly by tomorrow, but then I'll ask the witness a question or so about the transcript which we'll be able later to connect to the video. Here are the transcripts. It's Exhibit 330.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just before the attempt to play the video is made, Major, were you present at an oath-taking ceremony in Zenica in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Then we'll just have a look at this video, with the technical booth's assistance. But we may not see very much of it, because it's in very poor quality at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "DARIO KORDIC: Dear Croat soldiers, I greet you on behalf of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and also on behalf of the greatest son of the Croat people of Herceg-Bosna, president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Mate Boban. "I'm glad that we're here on Croat territory. You've heard these days the messages. They are telling us what we are fighting for -- for the liberation, for a political solution for the Croat people -- because we never again want to repeat the mistakes that were repeated in history. "Therefore, I would like to say, from this place, today on this ceremony of oath-giving of this brigade, Jure Francetic, that these Croat soldiers are brave, as the previous speakers have said, and that we shall certainly, with full hearts and souls, carry out this task which is placed in front of us by the generations of Croat soldiers of the past centuries and our families and children. So long live all. Merry Christmas and Christmas holidays and for Za Dom Spremni."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were there. Do you still maintain from even that speech and that appearance that Mr. Kordic had nothing whatsoever to do with the military?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how do you interpret what he's saying there about fighting for this and that? How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: What he said was pure politics. He addressed people in a political way; that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the transcript, it says: "We are fighting for a political solution. We're fighting for liberation and for a political solution because we never again want to repeat the mistakes that were repeated in history. Therefore, we want to liberate all the occupied territories, return all that which is ours, and Jajce and Kupres, and Komusina and Posavina, to liberate once and for all the Croat territory, Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna, which no one will take away from us, so that this will for centuries be ours." You don't feel there's any even remote suggestion of military activity in any of that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I already said that from the top of his address and all the way down, it's all political. In this excerpt, I see nothing military, nor did I sense any of that when I was down there in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You saw General Praljak there, of course, to the right of the screen, I think.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that General Praljak was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You saw him around Zenica from time to time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He, of course, was a Croat general, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No. He was the commander of the Main Staff of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's move to 1993. You were still in Zenica. Did you have any recollection or do you have any recollection of any bombs going off in the area of the Radio Zenica building at about New Year's Eve in 1992?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 1993, you will have started a new series of communications, of written communications to various bodies; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that the serial numbers will start off with number 1 of 1993 and go up; number 2, number 3, number 4, and so on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It won't be the case when I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if you could help us at all with roughly how many written communications in any form or series, however they were numbered, how many such communications you would be sending out per week. Give us an idea.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number. I'm telling you, it all depends on the situation and developments on the ground. So sometimes you would send 30 such documents a day, and the next day not a single one. I'm telling you, it all depended on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to look, just for clarification, please, at a document, new Exhibit 672.2A, or 672.2, actually. Now, this is a document for which we have a translation, and we have a translation of the date. But if you would look at the date on the original, which I'd ask the Chamber to do as well, it's not entirely clear. It's sixteen o something 1993, and then the number of the document appears to be -- well, it looks as if it's some figure, and then "69 of 93". That's the only things we've got. If we come to the English translation, Major, I can tell you how it's been translated or deciphered as to date. It's been suggested that it's the 16th of April, with a query, 1993, and that there is an indecipherable number followed by "69 of 93". Now, first we can see the numbering system and we can see that this is over your name. Is this a document of yours, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: It could be my document, because there is my signature. But it could have also been typed by somebody else, because there is no actual signature, even though my name is indicated. Just a moment, just a moment. If I may, Your Honours, in my documents I always put the initials of the person who wrote the document. So somewhere in this document should be my initials, capital D, small A, capital G. And then once again the same thing, I don't see it on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, the document itself goes from the Jure Francetic Brigade command to the head of the Vitez something, Tomo Krizanac. Can you tell us who it's to, then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Tomo Krizanac was the head of the Military Intelligence Service in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And we see the message is short: "Please submit data regarding events in Vitez." Well, now, is that a typical message of the type you would be sending on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I already told you that we exchanged some information at meetings, and also we exchanged information in this form at my request.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The translation suggests, with a question mark, that it's the 16th of April, and we can't read the first digit of the number of the series. Do you think this was the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As far as I can read, it's not really very visible. I should say it was the 16th of January, 1993, and the figure below is "569-93".

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's why I was asking you originally about how many documents you would send a day or a week. Is it really the case that by the end of the second week of January, you would already have sent 569 documents?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The records of our unit were formed in December 1992, after the Jure Francetic Brigade was set up, and it was as of that date that we began to send documents on the basis of new files, of new records. It had nothing to do with the end of the year, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You can remember that now, can you, that "569 of 93" really means 569 document starting in December of 1992; can you really remember that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I shall merely repeat. You're guessing at the date and at the figure, and whether I can remember that particular figure, that particular digit, hardly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are obviously two possibilities. One is that this document was sent, as has been interpreted or deciphered, on the 16th of April. I wondered what reason there might be to send information from Vitez on the 16th of April, please, Major.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I shall say it once again. The date, if it is the 16th of April --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was a question. If you don't know, just say you don't know. But don't keep saying, "I've said it already."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall take that as an, "I don't know," I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Between January and March of 1993, then, you were in Zenica, and as we can reasonably guess from this document, sending, at least for six weeks, something in the region of 500 communications in a six-week period, as a possibility. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although, of course, some of those documents might have been lost when you left Zenica, they would also all exist in copy form at the other end, wouldn't they, unless they had been destroyed there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I suppose there must be documentation at the place to which I was sending it, except that I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any efforts made, either for the giving of your evidence or any efforts made at all, to try to track down the documents that must have passed between the intelligence services of one town and another and that will clearly document events from the HVO perspective? Are you aware of any efforts made to try and get hold of those documents, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, just give me one minute, please. Your Honour, I have a document that I haven't yet had copied or yet presented for formal translation, and it's my error, of course. It was available to me. But can I ask the witness to look at the original of it or the Croat language version of it, place the English version of an unofficial translation on the ELMO, and get Ms. Verhaag to give it a number, and we'll produce it and get additional copies in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you have the original of the document that we are seeing on the screen there, Major. It's dated the 21st of March of 1993, and it's a proposal for reconnaissance and monitoring. And it reads, as we can see, that: "Considering that in the responsibility zone of the Brigade Francetic, there are no aggressive activities or confrontation along the line in relation to an order, and for the purpose of monitoring of ABiH movements and their grouping, I propose ..." And then at the last entry number 4: "Reports to be submitted daily, ref. VOS by battalions, or personally to the aide of the chief of brigade for VOS." And then it's got a typed signature: "A. To the chief of brigade for VOS, Darko Gelic." Do you remember that order or that proposal?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that can just inform us of the volume of paperwork that there must have been covering the HVO's perception of events as they developed. On a daily basis, there were to be reports, if that proposal was to be accepted?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, since there is no number up there at the top, it means that the proposal was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The letter was sent or the proposal was sent somewhere, but you say that the fact that it was not numbered means nobody acted on it. Was it roughly once a day, nevertheless, that there were reports prepared?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I sent my reports, depending on the developments on the ground, once, twice, three times, or maybe 30 times a day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Move on, please, to Ahmici itself and to what was happening in Zenica. You were still in Zenica. What did you know of the build-up to the events in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about the preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At the time of Ahmici, you were in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I've got a couple of documents I may want to show you that come in between that, but they are not available at the moment so I'll have to come back to that, and I apologise for that. You were in Zenica, doing your normal job?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: These fall on the ground in Zenica at the beginning of April?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what do you say was the developing pattern of violence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: There were targeted operations of the army of B and H units. Their task was to first try to undercut -- to reduce the combat power of the Croat forces or, rather, the Croat Defence Council. And another task was to provoke incidents, to arrest the highest-ranking officers, so as to leave the Croat Defence Council without the commanders. And there were such instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that, because I think I can properly now revert to chronological ordering of events -- I hope so -- but with just one other intervening question. You've spoken of your knowledge of other places in communications. Were you aware of any attack on Busovaca in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell us, who was the attack by and who was the attack on?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The units of the 3rd Corps of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina launched the attack from the direction of Zenica and Kacuni and the Lasva on Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
