utterances.text: You're genuinely saying that that is where the attack came from. Can you account for the attack on Muslim premises or Muslim shops in that town in any way from the intelligence coming to you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I was receiving only intelligence information corroborating the fact that prior to these attacks, the Muslims had left the area of Busovaca. And most of those people, as I have already said, tended to move to villages around Busovaca, and they simply moved to Busovaca. They were not expelled, they were not banished from it, they simply moved to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What about attacks on premises, on Muslim businesses; can you account for that at all from what you learned by way of intelligence, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I did not get such information about attacks on Muslim facilities, business outlets.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to trouble you further with that, because that wasn't your immediate area at the time. Can we now look at a new document, 557.2. Sorry, 606. I'm sorry. I'm sorry about the quality of the original. It's not very strong. We'll put the English version on the ELMO, and I hope that if you can listen over the headphones, the nature of the document will become clear. This is dated the 5th of April of 1993, and we can see it's an invitation and it's signed by Dario Kordic and Kostroman and Valenta, and we see it goes to the vice-presidents and presidents and secretaries of the municipal boards of the HDZ of various places. And then in the next entry it goes to presidents, vice-presidents and secretaries of the HVO municipalities, and Zenica is referred to there. And it's an invitation to attend a meeting on Thursday, the 8th of April, which will be chaired by Mr. Kordic. What do you say, if anything, to the fact that the HVO governments are referred to in this invitation? Would you have got to know of this invitation yourself?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: HVO governments operated in all municipalities. They were politically structured governments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would you have got to know this?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But just so that we can clarify the position, the HVO government in a local municipality would be responding to an invitation from Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you don't suggest, do you, that the local military would be responding to the local HVO government in any particular way?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you still say you simply don't know who, if anyone, in the political chain exercised control over the military?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you that. I don't know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might, this was one of the residual documents that was outstanding at the end of the Prosecution's case and we were awaiting a translation of it. I hate to interrupt, but I have no idea how the first and second items on the agenda could be translated, since they are completely illegible. I wonder if there's a more legible copy of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There must be a better copy, and it's just that I haven't been able to retrieve it in the short time available. But yes, you're quite right; there must be a better one in order for the full translation to be there. I'll do our best to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, although I may have to come back to one small point in this part of the sequence, Major. In April, then, you knew nothing of what was going to happen at Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You would have been in daily communication with Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would it be important for someone in your intelligence position to be aware of troop movements that were planned in another municipality, or not?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Naturally, I should have known about it, and of course I would be interested in receiving such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so are you telling us that you weren't alerted to any troop movements, just so that we can have the picture clear?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. And then you say there was an attack, or there was fighting in Zenica starting when?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And what, if any, part did you take in that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What part did you take in it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: When we were pulling out from the command post, lock, stock, and barrel, with the protective forces who were there, and that would be a company or something, we pulled out to Zmajevac. We tried to organise our defence. And we were to link up without forces which were at Stranjani and then at Onak. But since the forces at Stranjani had already retreated towards Onak, there was nobody that we could link up with, and we remained alone at Zmajevac. Then we headed for Cajdras, where both troops and civilians gathered. There were around 3.000 people all together: women, children, civilians, soldiers, everybody together. And most of those soldiers surrendered to the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and they were later on taken to the penitentiary at Zenica, imprisoned, some of them to the ill-famed musical school, and some other places which we didn't know about and we didn't know where people were. I did not surrender, so that I stayed there. And that was how I participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how many days did this account for, roughly?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: All together, between the attack and surrender, one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And how far were you from Zenica at the time of the surrender? Just tell the Judges and me so that we can know roughly how far it is.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: From the town of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I was at about, roughly, from the centre of the town, some 15, 16 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Had you by this time -- presumably you had -- heard of the kidnapping of Totic, and Kordic speaking about that at a press conference?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: That was before the attack of the ABiH units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And as to the alleged attack by the ABiH units, isn't the position -- or is the position this: Far from them attacking, in fact it was the HVO that engaged in an attack on this day, however ill-advised?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, this was not some alleged ABiH attack against the HVO; it was a direct attack with a well-known objective. Not an alleged attack of the army; it was a direct one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And are you saying that ABiH soldiers would have been visible to international observers at about that time in Zenica and in the area of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The international monitors and all the international organisations that were in Zenica were in the Hotel Internacional. That is where there were headquarters. All roads leading to Zenica during the attack of ABiH against the HVO were completely blocked. Nobody could move anywhere. I doubt that anybody from any international organisation could have had any access there. However, after the fall of Zenica and after we arrived in Cajdras, the BritBat Battalion of UNPROFOR forces arrived. I don't know -- it was a motorised platoon, but I don't know who was their commander. We asked them to protect the people and to help us move to Vitez. They firmly refused it and went back to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to suggest to you that Cajdras was a sensible place to retreat to after the attack by Blaskic on the metallurgical facility had come to an unhappy end, so far as the Croats were concerned, that that's the reality.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The attack against the metallurgical facility?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, these comments on the part of the Prosecutor are misplaced. The HVO never attacked any ABiH unit in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, after that one day that you've spoken of, you were still at liberty?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I was at liberty throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where did you go next?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I went to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Straight away, or did you go back to Zenica first, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I first hid in the surrounding villages from Mala Broda, Broda, and that area, and then went on to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where were you, do you think, on the 19th of April, the 18th of April? 19th of April, then.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think that I was hiding from the Mujahedin in order not to be captured by them in Mala Broda.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, there was a shelling on Zenica, wasn't there? You know that?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know the date. It could have been the 19th or the 20th. But I know of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you know anything of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: About shelling?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I only heard those shells whizzing by and falling.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's just get that. Where are you? To the west, the north, the east, or the south?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: North-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. And you can say you actually heard them whizzing, can you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Anybody could hear a shell if it flies over you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those shells were coming from the west, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you the estimate where it came from, because, first of all, I do not know where it came from. I can only make guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, those shells needed someone to guide them to their target in Zenica, on the evidence we've heard, somebody with military experience. Were there HVO soldiers and officers left in Zenica after this battle that you speak of?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I can serve as an example. I had remained in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you eventually got to Vitez, did you document your movements from the time that you had left Zenica? Did you make a record of what had happened and where you had been?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The entire period between the Zenica HVO fall until I left the area, I put down in writing all the facts as to what had befallen the Croats in those days. I also listed the reasons why things happen. I wrote all this down.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And that document is where?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This isn't the document, the diary, that you let your son write over?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And obviously a document like this, you would recognise, as a military man, would be an important document?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's no reason to believe that the archive of Vitez, to which this document may have gone, would have been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I said that I really did not know what happened to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And yet even when preparing to give evidence here today, you didn't yourself make any efforts to track down such an important document, did you?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I did not. I did not search for this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I wonder if the witness could just see Exhibit 812.1, please. Sorry not to have given you advance notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a document of yours.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a document of yours. It comes from the ECMM regional centre in Zenica. Did you have dealings with the ECMM before you left Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were aware of their existence there and aware of what they were doing in your territory generally?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you find, from what you knew of them on intelligence, did you find the ECMM to be a reliable source of information and intelligence and assessment?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: If they were in the right place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, this reporting monitor, for the period 17th to the 24th of April of 1993, covering Zenica and areas elsewhere, of course, says -- and maybe you understand English. I'm not sure. But he says this, in summary: that the clear position of the authorities to implement the Vance-Owen Plan, pressing the Muslim population to leave the so-called provinces, provoked their reaction with very strong and cruel fighting and actions against the civilian population. Now, is that the reality of what happened? You were there as an intelligence officer. Was it the Vance-Owen Plan and the possibility of enforcing it that led to reaction?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: What this gentleman wrote down in this report did not reflect reality. As far as I know, the Croats did sign the Vance-Owen Plan, but it was never implemented, and the reasons for its nonimplementation I think again lie squarely with the politicians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: From neither your Zenica position nor from your next Vitez position, because you had two different perspectives, did you see anything to support this suggestion that it was the pressure to have the Vance-Owen Plan that led to reaction and to the unhappy violence?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was signed by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May he see, please, Exhibit 832.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When you were in Vitez, was there still the possibility to communicate with HVO soldiers left in Zenica, if there were any?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you do to rely on for intelligence coming from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: The source of information for an intelligence officer is not just a regular soldier. And on the other side, when I arrived in Vitez, I had already had done some intelligence work, but I ceased that work and I became a liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you nevertheless continue to receive some information, as one of the comparatively senior officers in Hotel Vitez, coming from your former town?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Such information as I was able to gather I obviously did process, because it is a duty of every officer to transmit the information that he receives, as is the duty of any soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If you look at this document, paragraph 2, which is a daily report on a man called Morsink, and it's for the 26th of April, so it's still at the end of -- well, you're now in Vitez, but I'd just like your comment on this, as somebody from Zenica. He says, at paragraph 2, in short, that they heard of the HVO in Travnik ordering refugees from going back to their houses and saying they had to go to Nova Bila. That is, I think, refugees who were heading back to Zenica. Can you explain why that was happening at that time you were there, broadly?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: These are only words put down on a piece of paper. This was not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You're saying that this officer must have got this completely wrong?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, that's a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In Vitez, what were you told about what had happened at Ahmici, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: We never spoke about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me see if I understand that. Do you mean it was never spoken about, as a matter of fact, or do you mean that there was some clear policy that it would not be spoken about?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I mention no policy. I just said that we never spoke about it at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You must have become aware at some stage that something had happened in Ahmici that was regarded by a wider observing population than just Central Bosnia as an outrage. When did you become aware that something had happened that was regarded as an outrage, Major, please?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: You see, I only heard about Ahmici from certain stories, what had happened. These were just stories and rumours. But time flew by while I was in Vitez, and every day brought something new. You had the same scenes repeated every day. Attacks were a daily occurrence. So each one of us first was focused on what was happening on that day rather than what had happened the day before.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you not aware that the international observers were carrying out an inquiry or had carried out an inquiry into Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I didn't know, even though these European Monitors and all others did communicate with me on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any proper inquiry being conducted for Colonel Blaskic about what had happened at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I didn't know until this Tribunal got involved in this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But as liaison officer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: When are you going to finish, Mr. Nice, please? The Chamber is concerned about the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I shall finish quite shortly, and I shall finish, with the Chamber's leave, when I've concluded the questions that I'm going to ask. There are not very many more, but they are important. I have to say that if we are going to be permanently under the timetable pressure, it's going to make our job very difficult. It's difficult enough as it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It is difficult to complete a case of this sort in a reasonable time. It requires the cooperation of counsel. We dealt with the cross-examination of the Defence by requiring them to conclude within a timetable. It seems to me that it is only fair that the Prosecution should be treated in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I am certainly not going beyond a reasonable period of time. I have to say we feel already that we are under very considerable pressure to take things too quickly. It is extremely difficult, coming to this material, when the material comes to us late. Cross-examination, it may not immediately be obvious why, is here to help you, not to help us, and I will repeat the difficulties I find myself in if I am over-hurried. I will do my best to complete this afternoon, if the Chamber gives me a little more time. I cannot guarantee that I will do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: For sure, this afternoon we do not have the time. We have to rise at 4.00. No doubt that will give you this evening to tailor your cross-examination, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Let me just see where I was. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a liaison officer, it would have been extremely important for you to be able to assure international observers that matters concerning them were being dealt with properly; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: With -- I spoke very openly, correctly, with not only the monitors but any other international representatives, and it wasn't just my passing on my own opinions. They could have come to their own conclusions based on what I communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think you're missing the point, and I want to press you on this as my last question on the topic and before I move on. But the question is this: If Blaskic had been conducting -- or having conducted a proper, careful inquiry into the massacre that we know happened at Ahmici, it would be pretty important for him to know that you could tell the International Community that things were being done properly, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I told you that I did not know about the Ahmici case; nor did anyone from an international organisation ask me any question regarding that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And nor did Blaskic tell you that he had commissioned an inquiry?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I see no reason for him to have done so, because this had happened before I assumed the duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May Exhibit 2546 go on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Would that be about June of 1993?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall this period, what date exactly this was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that on the road to Tisovac or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: That is at Tisovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You went there from time to time, what, to see Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Why should I go to see Kordic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Why did you go there, then?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I went there to Tisovac altogether twice, and I believe the reason for at least one of these visits is obvious in this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, that's a social side to it on this occasion. But you went there on other occasions. What was it to see, if not Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I told you, I went to Tisovac once or twice, maybe three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All for social reasons or for other reasons?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: From what I can tell in this photograph, these were not social reasons, these were business reasons, because an officer of the British Battalion, and I think that he was the liaison officer, insisted on it. The second time, I think the occasion was similar for my going to Tisovac. And whether I had been there for a third time, that I question myself, and I may have contacted with a gentleman in the photograph on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What other troops or units were stationed up at Tisovac, apart from Kordic's own headquarters?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I don't know. As far as I can recall, the facility where I went was not Kordic's headquarters at all, it was something else completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. In the interests of speed, I'll move to Exhibit 881.1, please. This is a document, the version of which says it's the 3rd of May but has been written over "the 3rd of June", and the information I want you to look at on this milinfosum number 35 relates to paragraph 4, Vitez, where the Vitez liaison officer, who would be the man Whitworth of whom you have spoken, confirms the following details on the 4th Battalion HVO Military Police, also known as the Jokers, sets out that they were commanded by Ljubicic, with deputy commander Kosic. That's accurate, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Pasko Ljubicic was for a period of time, but I don't know until when, and I really don't know who his deputy was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It then says they apparently come under the direct control of Dario Kordic and are under the local control of Tihomir Blaskic, and it makes a comment. Now, Whitworth spoke to you quite a lot, didn't he? Didn't he?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: Yes, he spoke a lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there was nobody else, apart from you as the base liaison officer, to speak to at that time and in that area, was there?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I think that the British Battalion liaison officer communicated a lot, not only with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he get that information and did he form that view as a result of something that you told him about Kordic?

utterances.speaker: DARKO GELIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know on the basis of what he was forming his conclusions. He couldn't have done so on the basis of his talks with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that a convenient moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Major Gelic, will you be back, please, tomorrow morning at half past 9 to conclude your evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.03 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 3rd day of May, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
